questions.question: What are the React+TypeScript contracts — props (children!), event types, hooks, and discriminated-union state?
questions.title: React Ts Contracts
questions.direct_answer: The core contracts: PROPS as a type (interface ButtonProps extends React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> — INHERIT the native element's props for polymorphic wrappers; children: React.ReactNode — NOT ReactElement — the renderable union; optional with ?/partial generic); EVENT types (React events are synthetic wrappers: React.FormEvent, React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> for inputs, React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement> — the generic IS the currentTarget element type, which makes e.currentTarget typed and e.target honestly broad; keyboard: React.KeyboardEvent + the key discriminants); HOOKS (useState<T> for the FULL lifecycle union — useState<'idle'|'saving'|'error'>("idle") over booleans; the functional updater's parameter is typed; useRef<T | null>(null) for DOM refs — the null-before-mount reality); and DISCRIMINATED UNIONS for state/props (variant: 'primary' | 'ghost' with variant-dependent fields — one runtime discriminant narrows the whole shape: impossible combinations become unrepresentable — the single most valuable pattern in React TS).

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: The core contracts: PROPS as a type (interface ButtonProps extends React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> — INHERIT the native element's props for polymorphic wrappers; children: React.ReactNode — NOT ReactElement — the renderable union; optional with ?/partial generic); EVENT types (React events are synthetic wrappers: React.FormEvent, React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> for inputs, React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement> — the generic IS the currentTarget element type, which makes e.currentTarget typed and e.target honestly broad; keyboard: React.KeyboardEvent + the key discriminants); HOOKS (useState<T> for the FULL lifecycle union — useState<'idle'|'saving'|'error'>("idle") over booleans; the functional updater's parameter is typed; useRef<T | null>(null) for DOM refs — the null-before-mount reality); and DISCRIMINATED UNIONS for state/props (variant: 'primary' | 'ghost' with variant-dependent fields — one runtime discriminant narrows the whole shape: impossible combinations become unrepresentable — the single most valuable pattern in React TS).

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    CP[ComponentProps native] --> FREE[native props inherited + typed]
    CH[children: ReactNode] --> ALL[strings numbers fragments null — renderable]
    EV[ChangeEvent of T] --> CT[currentTarget typed as T — target honest]
    ST[useState union state] --> NOFLAGS[no boolean combos; typos = compile errors]
    DU[discriminated union] --> NARROW[one discriminant narrows the shape]
    DU2[variant props: link vs button] --> IMPOSSIBLE[illegal combos unrepresentable]
    GEN[generic component] --> ADAPT[T flows from items prop]
    REF[useRef T null] --> MOUNT[null before mount — optional-chain access]
    SC[server components] --> NOEV[no event handlers — interactions in client children]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The synthetic event model (why the generics look like they do): React pools and normalizes native events behind SyntheticEvent — a uniform interface across browsers, with currentTarget typed by the generic (the HANDLER's element) while target is the actual hit node (honestly broad — a span inside the button). That distinction is the answer to 'why does e.currentTarget.value work but e.target.value error' — currentTarget carries the generic's type; event delegation and nested-hit realities mean target must stay general.

The hook-type details that trip practitioners: useState's type argument is the VALUE's shape — for lazy initialization pass a function returning the shape: useState(() => parseInitial()) (the initializer-generic overload); the functional updater receives the CURRENT state type — setState(s => s + 1) with s: number inferred, but with a union the updater must return the FULL union (partial updates need the spread with a type-level assist); useReducer types the reducer itself ((state, action) => state) and the ACTION union drives the discriminated state machine — the reducer pattern and the union pattern are the same idea at different layers. And the effect cleanup discipline: useEffect's teardown must be void | Destructor — returning anything else (an async function returning a promise) is the classic 'return type of useEffect callback must be void or destructor' error — the async-effect wrapper pattern exists because of it.

The module-boundary typing (the modern layer): type your PROPS at the component boundary and let inference flow INSIDE — the same principle as functions. ComponentProps<'form'> / ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> (the WithoutRef family resolves the ref-type collision with your own) are the polymorphic-wrapper enablers; the forwardRef generics (<HTMLInputElement, Props>) are the ref-forwarding contract (React 19 deprecates forwardRef — ref becomes a plain prop: the migration edge worth one sentence); and satisfies on the props literal ({ variant: 'primary' } satisfies VariantProps) validates without widening — the pattern that keeps literal discriminants narrow through prop chains. The through-line: React+TS's value is ONE idea — make the state machine and the prop contracts unrepresentable-wrong.
